final.title: Scope creep is usually a boundary problem
final.body:
If you run a one-person business, scope creep is usually not a motivation problem. It is a workflow boundary problem: work expands when nothing says where the task starts, where it stops, and what gets deferred.

So I would treat it as a decision problem, not a personality problem. Pick one recurring task that keeps pulling you away from core work: customer questions, invoice data entry, or lead follow-up. Then ask two things. Does it repeat often enough to describe in steps? Does it have a measurable outcome? If the answer is no, automation is probably the wrong tool. If the answer is yes, a bounded automation may be better than another afternoon of manual work or the not-so-small matter of hiring.

That is also how our diagnostic is meant to work: identify one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and only then define a narrow pilot scope. The point is not to force AI into every task. Human approval still belongs anywhere money moves or the decision is high risk.

If you want a practical self-check, use this: which task do you repeat most often that someone else could complete without needing your judgement every time?

final.title: Scope creep is often a boundary problem
final.body:
If you run a one-person business, scope creep is usually not a motivation problem. It is a workflow boundary problem: work keeps expanding because nothing says where the task starts, where it stops, and what gets deferred.

The practical decision is not “can AI do everything?” It is: which recurring task is pulling you away from core work, and is it stable enough to define clearly? A good candidate is something that repeats often, has a measurable outcome, and can be described step by step. Customer questions, invoice data entry, and lead follow-up are the kind of work to look at. If the task is ad hoc or high-risk, automation is probably the wrong tool.

That matters because the choice is usually between a bounded automation investment, more manual work, or hiring. For some owners, the recurring workload is large enough that it feels like a small business of its own. That is a joke with bad hygiene, but the decision is still real.

A sensible first step is to name one loop you repeat most often and ask: what can be handled by a clear rule, what still needs human approval, and what should be left alone? For money movement and anything sensitive, the answer stays human. Start there, then keep the scope narrow.
